---
title: "Seasonality"
---

```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(scales)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))

focus <- c("Fungi", "Plants", "Birds", "Insects")
month_breaks <- c(1, 5, 9, 14, 18, 22, 27, 31, 35, 40, 44, 48)

obs <- read_csv(here("data", "processed", "observations.csv"),
                show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(week_of_year = pmin(week_of_year, 52L))   # fold week 53 into 52

effort <- read_csv(here("data", "processed", "effort_total_weekly.csv"),
                   show_col_types = FALSE)
```

## Observer effort

Observations per week climb with the number of observers, and both have a strong
seasonal rhythm of their own. That is why raw counts can't be read as biology.

```{r effort}
effort |>
  filter(week_start >= as.Date("2018-01-01")) |>
  ggplot(aes(week_start, observations, colour = stateProvince)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Observations per week", colour = NULL)
```

## Effort-adjusted seasonality

For each state and group, the index is the group's share of its yearly observations
falling in a given week, divided by the share of *all* observations falling in that
week. Above 1 (red) = over-represented relative to overall effort.

```{r index}
weekly <- obs |>
  filter(group %in% focus) |>
  count(stateProvince, group, week_of_year, name = "n") |>
  complete(stateProvince, group, week_of_year = 1:52, fill = list(n = 0)) |>
  group_by(stateProvince, group) |>
  mutate(group_share = n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup()

all_week <- obs |>
  count(stateProvince, week_of_year, name = "n_all") |>
  complete(stateProvince, week_of_year = 1:52, fill = list(n_all = 0)) |>
  group_by(stateProvince) |>
  mutate(all_share = n_all / sum(n_all)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(stateProvince, week_of_year, all_share)

index <- weekly |>
  left_join(all_week, by = c("stateProvince", "week_of_year")) |>
  mutate(rel_index = group_share / all_share)
```

```{r heatmap}
#| fig-height: 8
index |>
  mutate(group = factor(group, levels = rev(focus))) |>
  ggplot(aes(week_of_year, group, fill = rel_index)) +
  geom_tile() +
  facet_wrap(~stateProvince, ncol = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = month_breaks, labels = month.abb,
                     expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2c7bb6", mid = "white", high = "#d7191c",
                       midpoint = 1, limits = c(0, 3), oob = squish,
                       name = "Relative\nindex") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

## Peak weeks

Peak week of the adjusted index, using only weeks with at least 20 observations
for that group and state so thin data doesn't create fake peaks.

```{r peaks}
index |>
  filter(n >= 20) |>
  group_by(stateProvince, group) |>
  slice_max(rel_index, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  transmute(State = stateProvince, Group = group,
            `Peak week` = week_of_year,
            `Approx. date` = format(as.Date("2025-01-01") + (week_of_year - 1) * 7,
                                    "%b %d"),
            Observations = n,
            Index = round(rel_index, 2)) |>
  arrange(State, Group) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

## Notes and next steps

- All years are pooled, so recent years (when iNaturalist grew fastest) carry the
  most weight. A sturdier version computes shares within each year and averages.
- Fungi and plants peak counts mix biology with observer behavior (for example,
  people hike more in fall). Comparing with eBird for birds is the next test.
